Stage 1 · Warm-up

Rules of the conversation

Every culture has rules about how people talk to each other. Almost none of them are ever said out loud.

💬🌍
1 · Read the four situations. Which one would be hardest for you to handle?
AYou are ten minutes into a meeting and the person opposite has answered every question directed at you.
BYou ask a new colleague a friendly question and the room goes quiet. Nobody tells you why.
CSomebody you have just met stands close enough that you keep stepping backwards without meaning to.
DYou finish speaking and nobody replies for eight seconds. Everyone else seems perfectly comfortable.

Choose one, then compare with a partner. Did you choose the same one, and for the same reason?Choose one and explain your reason to your teacher.Choose one and write two sentences explaining why.

3 · Read the claim. How far do you agree?
A claim

“Most cross-cultural misunderstandings are not caused by weak language. They are caused by people applying their own rules about silence, distance and directness to somebody else’s conversation — and never realising they have done it.”

2 · Complete the account with the words in the box. There are three words you will not need.

Click a word in the box, then click the gap you want it in. Click a filled gap to empty it.

I had been in São Paulo for three days when I managed to get almost everything wrong in a single evening. I was seated next to a woman called Luísa and for the first ten minutes we completely — the sort of conversation where you forget you are speaking a second language. Then, mistaking her ease for permission, I asked what she paid for her flat. What followed was one of those pauses that feel far longer than they are. I had put my , and I could see it in the faces around me before anybody said a word. At home the question is unremarkable; there it was intrusive enough to people who had known me for an hour. Later, a man opposite me the conversation for the better part of twenty minutes and nobody once him. What struck me was not his confidence but everyone else’s patience: they were listening , nodding and reacting, in a way that would have looked exaggerated where I grew up. Then he made a sign to call me over: he his index finger towards himself. In the town I come from, that is close to an insult. He meant nothing whatsoever by it, of course. Nobody had a , nobody was hurt, and the whole thing was a straightforward . But I walked home fairly certain that is the most demanding kind of talk there is, and the one nobody ever teaches you.

Click a word in the box, then click the gap you want it in. Click a filled gap to empty it.

Successful communication across cultures depends on far more than vocabulary. Physical distance varies widely: in Japan a respectful distance is around centimetres, while in North America two people who are not close friends stand about centimetres apart. Getting this wrong sends a signal in either direction — stand too close and you cause discomfort, stand too far away and you seem . Silence is read differently too. Where most Europeans and North Americans treat it as a sign, some East Asian cultures see it as a mark of . Volume follows a similar pattern, with speakers from southern Europe and South America tending to be . Topics carry the greatest risk. Questions about somebody’s are unlikely to be welcome, whereas sport, where a person is from and the are usually safe.

3 · Read the table.
TypeExampleWhat happens
Object questionWho did she offend?Auxiliary + subject + verb. The question word asks about the object.
Subject questionWho offended her?No auxiliary. The question word is the subject, so the order does not change.

1 · Read the explanation.
Subject and object questions

When the question word (who, what, which, how many) is the subject of the verb, you do not add do, does or did, and the word order stays the same as a statement: Who offended her? When the question word asks about the object, you add the auxiliary and put it before the subject: Who did she offend?

The two look almost identical but ask opposite things. Compare Who interrupted Ali? (Ali was speaking) with Who did Ali interrupt? (Ali was the one cutting in). Nothing in the words themselves tells you which is meant — only the presence or absence of the auxiliary does.

Questions inside a longer sentence

After phrases like Could you tell me…, Do you know…, I was wondering…, I’d like to know…, the question becomes part of a statement. Three things change:

  • the word order becomes statement order: where the meeting is, not where is the meeting;
  • do, does and did disappear, and their tense moves into the main verb: Why did she leave? → …why she left;
  • a yes/no question needs if or whether: Do you know if he speaks Kazakh?

The indirect version is longer, not more polite in itself — the politeness comes from the opening phrase.

12 · Read this before the extra practice.
Why the auxiliary disappears

English normally builds a question by putting an auxiliary in front of the subject: Did she offend anybody? That inversion only happens when there is a subject to move the auxiliary in front of. In a subject question the question word already occupies the subject slot, so there is nothing to invert and no auxiliary appears: Who offended her? The same applies to what, which, whose, how many, how much when they open the subject: Which flight leaves first? · How many people complained?

Two consequences B2 learners often miss. First, the verb after a subject who or what is singular by default: Who wants coffee? — even when you expect several people to answer. Second, the auxiliary comes back as soon as the question is negative: Who didn’t get the email? · What hasn’t been paid for? Do also returns for emphasis or contradiction: So who did pay, then?

Whom is the object form. It survives in formal writing and directly after a preposition (To whom should I address this?), but Who did she offend? is the standard spoken form and is not an error.

Questions folded into a longer sentence

After an opener such as Could you tell me…, Do you know…, I was wondering…, Have you any idea…, Would you mind telling me…, the question becomes a clause inside a statement. Three things happen, and only three:

  • the subject goes back in front of the verb: where the meeting is;
  • do / does / did disappears and its tense moves into the main verb: Where did she go? → …where she went;
  • a yes/no question needs if or whether, because there is no question word to link the clause: Do you know whether the office is open?

The tense itself never shifts — this is not reported speech. Do you know where he works? stays present. And the sentence takes a question mark only if the opener is a question: Could you tell me where it is? but I’d like to know where it is.

Fine detail: if or whether, and do you think

If and whether are interchangeable in most indirect yes/no questions, but only whether works: after a preposition (It depends on whether she agrees), before to + verb (I asked whether to wait), directly before or not (whether or not it matters), and at the start of a subject clause (Whether he meant it is another question). Whether is also the safer choice in writing, where if can be read as a condition.

With do you think / do you reckon / do you suppose, the question word moves to the very front and the opener keeps question order, while the clause after it takes statement order: Where do you think she went? — never Do you think where she went? Compare Do you know where she went?, where the whole thing can be answered yes or no. A do you think question cannot.

Errors to watch: Could you tell me where is the lift the lift is? · Do you know if does he speak he speaks Russian? · Who did write wrote this? · I wonder where did she go? she went.

1 · Read the model.
Model

Hi Marta,

Before you arrive, a few things nobody will explain to you. First, distance: colleagues here stand about half a metre apart, so if you step back, it reads as coldness rather than politeness. Second, silence. A pause of five or six seconds is normal in a meeting and nobody rushes to fill it — it is not an awkward silence, it just looks like one to a visitor.

You may be wondering whether there is anything you should avoid asking. There is: what people earn. It is the fastest way to put your foot in it, even with somebody you have hit it off with. Family and food are safe, and everybody makes small talk about the weather.

One last thing. Curling your finger to say ‘come here’ is close to an insult here; use your whole hand. Get that one wrong and the misunderstanding will outlast the conversation.

See you soon,
Aisulu
